title: Counting Bits
description: Brute force to optimized: recomputing each value independently versus a recurrence reusing smaller answers.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer n, return an array ans of length n plus 1, where ans[i] is the number of set bits in the binary representation of i, for every i from 0 to n.

blocks.text: Given an integer n, return an array ans of length n plus 1, where ans[i] is the number of set bits in the binary representation of i, for every i from 0 to n.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Running Tally Sheet of Lit Switches
blocks.text: Like keeping a tally sheet listing, for every number from 0 up to n, how many switches would be lit if that number were dialed in on a row of binary switches, building the whole sheet as efficiently as possible.

blocks.caption: Compute the set bit count for every integer from 0 up to n

blocks.text: With n equal to 0, the answer is simply the single element array [0], since 0 itself has no set bits.
It helps to ask whether each value from 0 to n truly needs its bit count computed completely independently, or whether smaller, already computed values can be reused.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The brute force treats every value i as an unrelated problem, running Number of 1 Bits' Brian Kernighan clearing trick from scratch on each one, even though consecutive integers are closely related in their binary form.

Observation 2: Shifting i right by one bit (i >> 1) is the same as dropping its lowest bit and dividing by 2, producing a smaller index whose set bit count has ALREADY been computed earlier in the very same array being built.

Observation 3: The set bit count of i is exactly the set bit count of i shifted right by one, plus 1 more if the dropped lowest bit itself was a 1, giving the recurrence ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i AND 1), a one line dynamic programming relationship.

Observation 4: Tracing n = 5 confirms it, ans[5] is built from ans[2] (already known to be 1) plus the lowest bit of 5, which is 1, giving 1 + 1 = 2, matching the direct count from binary 101, all without a single inner loop.
Recognizing that dropping the lowest bit of i produces a smaller index whose answer is already sitting in the same output array is what turns independent per-value work into a single linear pass.
For every integer from 0 to n, compute its own set bit count independently, using a technique like Brian Kernighan's algorithm.

items: For every value i from 0 to n, repeatedly clear its lowest set bit and count how many clears it takes.
Store that count at ans[i].

codes.python:
def count_bits(n):
    ans = []
    for i in range(n + 1):
        count = 0
        x = i
        while x != 0:                                           # recomputes the bit count from scratch for every i
            x &= (x - 1)
            count += 1
        ans.append(count)
    return ans


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n = 5
    print(count_bits(n))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Each value i is processed with its own independent inner loop, since nothing about earlier results is being reused yet.
A separate copy x of i is modified inside the inner loop so that i itself stays intact for indexing into ans.

blocks.text: Every value's bit count is computed directly and correctly using Brian Kernighan's technique.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), since each of the n plus 1 values takes up to O(log of that value) to process.
Space: O(n), for the output array (not counting this as extra since it is required).
Limitation: each value's bit count is computed entirely independently, ignoring that ans[i] can actually be derived directly from an already computed smaller value.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it reruns a full bit clearing loop for every single value, ignoring how closely related consecutive integers' binary forms are.

What shifting right by one reveals: i >> 1 is a smaller index whose set bit count is already sitting in the very array being filled in, since it is always computed earlier in the same left to right pass.

What the dropped bit contributes: the one bit lost by that shift is exactly i AND 1, either 0 or 1, and it needs to be added back on top of the smaller answer.

The core idea: ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i AND 1), a constant time recurrence per value instead of a full independent bit clearing loop.

Every integer i, when shifted right by one bit, drops its lowest bit and becomes i divided by 2 (integer division), a value already computed earlier in the array. The set bit count of i is exactly the set bit count of i shifted right by one, plus 1 if the bit that was dropped (the lowest bit of i) was itself a 1. This gives a simple recurrence: ans[i] equals ans[i shifted right by 1] plus (i AND 1).
Build the answer array using the recurrence ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1), reusing already computed smaller values.

blocks.caption: Optimized: each value reuses the already computed answer for half its value

blocks.text: Because the loop processes i in increasing order starting from 1, the value ans[i >> 1] is always already filled in by the time it is needed, since i >> 1 is strictly smaller than i for every i greater than 0, so the recurrence always reads a value that has already been correctly computed.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with constant work per value.
Space: O(n), for the output array, no extra space beyond that.

items: ans[0] is left at its initialized value of 0 and the loop starts from index 1, since 0 has no lowest bit to drop.
Every iteration does exactly one array lookup, one shift, one AND, and one addition, regardless of how many bits i actually has set.

blocks.text: This problem is a good example of recognizing that a seemingly independent per-element computation can actually be expressed as a recurrence on already computed smaller values, turning an O(n log n) brute force into a linear one pass solution.

items: Recomputing each value's bit count from scratch instead of noticing the direct recurrence relationship with a smaller, already computed index.
Getting the recurrence direction backwards, referencing ans[i] to compute ans[i >> 1] instead of the other way around.

blocks.text: State the recurrence in words first (drop the lowest bit, reuse its answer, add back whether that dropped bit was a 1) before writing the one line of code, since the insight is the valuable part here, not the syntax.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid recomputing bit counts from scratch", think: reuse ans[i >> 1], a smaller already computed value.
If the interviewer says "what is the relationship between i and i >> 1", think: i >> 1 drops exactly the lowest bit of i.
If the interviewer says "can this be O(n)", think: yes, via the DP recurrence, one constant time step per value.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n log n) time, O(n) space for the output.
Optimized: O(n) time, O(n) space for the output, no extra space beyond it.

items: Pattern: a dynamic programming recurrence over bit counts, ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1).
Core Idea: dropping the lowest bit of i produces a smaller index whose set bit count is already known, so only the dropped bit's own contribution needs to be added back.
Time: O(n log n) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized recurrence.
Space: O(n) for the output array in both approaches, no extra space in the optimized version.
Most Important Observation: a per-element computation that looks independent can often be rewritten as a recurrence referencing a smaller, already computed answer.
Interview Difficulty: the brute force is easy; spotting the shift-and-reuse recurrence unprompted is the mark of a strong answer.
One line memory trick: ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1), reuse the smaller half, add back the dropped bit.
